content: Powered toothbrushes were first introduced to the market in the 1960s. A recent systematic review has indicated that certain types of powered toothbrushes are more effective than manual toothbrushes in reducing plaque and gingivitis. However, that review did not allow for direct comparisons between different types of powered toothbrushes. The objective of this study was to compare various modes of powered toothbrushes with one another in terms of their ability to reduce plaque and improve gingival health. Additional factors considered included their effectiveness in removing calculus and stains, their cost, reliability, and any adverse effects associated with their use. To gather relevant data, the researchers searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group's Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL. These searches were conducted up to July 26, 2010, and no language restrictions were applied. The inclusion criteria for the trials were as follows: participants had to be randomly allocated to groups, they could not have compromised manual dexterity, and they had to use powered toothbrushes unsupervised for a minimum of four weeks. The primary outcomes assessed were plaque and gingivitis scores after the trial period. Data extraction was performed independently by multiple reviewers to ensure accuracy. When data were missing, the authors of the trials were contacted to provide the necessary information. The effect size for each meta-analysis was calculated using the standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), employing a random-effects model. Potential sources of heterogeneity were also evaluated. The review included data from 17 trials involving a total of 1,369 participants. Evidence from seven trials, which lasted up to three months and were at unclear or high risk of bias, suggested that rotation-oscillation toothbrushes were more effective than side-to-side toothbrushes in reducing plaque (SMD 0.24; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.46) and gingivitis (SMD 0.35; 95% CI -0.04 to 0.74). However, the difference was small, and its clinical significance remains uncertain. Due to the limited number of trials, no definitive conclusions could be drawn about the superiority of other modes of powered toothbrushes. Only minor and temporary side effects were reported, and no data were available on cost or reliability. In conclusion, there is some evidence to suggest that rotation-oscillation toothbrushes may reduce plaque and gingivitis more effectively than side-to-side toothbrushes in the short term. However, the clinical importance of this difference is unclear. Further high-quality trials are needed to determine whether other modes of powered toothbrushes offer superior benefits.
